title: Morse Code
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 28–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Morse Code

Morse code is being replaced by a new satellitebased system for sending distress calls at sea. Its dots and dashes have had a good run for their money.

Paragraph A

A A Since 1992, countries around the world have been decommissioning their Morse equipment with similar (if less poetic) signoffs as the world's shipping switches over to a new satellitebased arrangement，the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System. The final deadline for the switchover to GMDSS is February 1st, a date that is widely seen as the end of an era.

Paragraph B

B B The code has, however, had a good history. Appropriate for a technology commonly associated with radio operators on sinking ships，the idea of Morse code is said to have occurred to Samuel Morse while he was on board a ship crossing the Atlantic. At the time Morse was a painter and occasional inventor, but when one of the ship's passengers informed him of recent advances in electrical theory, Morse was suddenly taken with the idea of building an electric telegraph to send message in codes. Other inventors had been trying to do just that for the best part of a century. Morse succeeded and is now remembered as ‘the father of the telegraph’ partly thanks to his single mindedness — it was 12 years, for example, before he secured money from Congress to build his first telegraph line—but also for technical reasons.

Paragraph C

C C Unlike its competitor, electric telegraph design like needle telegraph that was built in Britain by Charles Wheatstone and William Cooke, Morse telegraph was straightforward: you need no more than a ‘sounder’ for incoming messages and a ‘key’—springloaded switch for outgoing information, and a wire to connect the duo. The operators need to learn some special dashes and dots which points to his name before they could effectively operate the hardware despite being simple. Interestingly, Morse has no intention of combining dots and dashes to form letters. Morse believed that messages could consist of numbers which correspond to words or sentences in a unique number dictionary. Thus, his first code, which was sketched in his book during the intercontinental voyage, was made up of dashes and dots which represented 09. However, Morse neglected the scheme for the Morse alphabet that could represent letters in dots and dashes, which he devised with the assistance of Alfred Vail, one of his associates.

Paragraph D

D D Compared to other userfriendly telegraph designs, the need to know the complicated code made Morse telegraph very tricky to use when it was released to the public. For instance, you can pick out letters using five needles on a diamondshaped grid when using the Cooke's and Wheatstone's telegraph. Though anybody could use the Cooke's telegraph; it needed five wires to connect to the telegraph stations while Morse' telegraph required only one. As it became popular, some people started developing a natural ability for the Morse code.

Paragraph E

E E Morse telegraph became the dominant of the traditional telegraphs in the early 1850s when electric telegraphy began. In 1851, it became the European standard for telegraphyconnecting directly to telegraph networks in other countries. Britain, unlike the other European countries, stuck to needle telegraphs for some years more. At this time, Morse code had been reviewed to include other foreign characters and accents. This review created an international version of it; thus we have American and International Morse code which still exists up till today.

Paragraph F

F F A rank which was based on how fast operators could receive and send the Morse code was evolving. The firstclass operators were the best paid in cities as they could handle huge traffic, and send and receive at the speed of 45 words/minute. The least paid were the inexperienced and slow operators who worked as parttimers in the rural areas. To a rural operator, the improved Morse code was the passport to a highly paid job in the city. The number of telegraphers in the middle classes had increased. Telegraphy is suitable for both sexes. As of 1870, women made up a third of the operators in the largest telegraph office in America, Western Union Office, New York.

Paragraph G

G G In a dramatic ceremony in 1871, Morse himself said goodbye to the global community of telegraphers he had brought into being. By the time of his death in 1872, the world was well and truly wired: more than 650000 miles of telegraph line and 30000 miles of submarine cable were throbbing with Morse code; and 20000 towns and villages were connected to the global network.

Paragraph H

H H But by the 1890s, the Morse telegraph's heyday as a cuttingedge technology was coming to an end, with the invention of the telephone and the rise of automatic telegraphs, precursors of the teleprinter, neither of which required specialist skills to operate. Morse code, however, was about to be given a new lease of life thanks to another new technology: wireless. Following the invention of radiotelegraphy by Guglielmo Marconi in 1896, its potential for use at sea quickly became apparent. For the first time, ships could communicate with each other, and with the shore, whatever the weather and even when out of visual range. In 1897 Marconi successfully sent Morse code messages between a shore station and an Italian warship 19 km (12 miles) away. By 1910, Morse radio equipment was commonplace on ships.

Questions 28–35

Reading Passage 3 has eight paragraphs, A-H.

Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.

List of Headings
I The advantage of Morse's invention
II A suitable job for women
III The improvement of Morse's invention
IV Sea rescue after the invention of radiotelegraphy
V The emergence of many job opportunities
VI Standard and variations
VII Application of Morse code in a new technology
VIII The discovery of electricity for business purpose
IX Global expansion of Morse Code
X The beginning of an end
XI The move of using code to convey information

Questions 36–40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

Choose

YESif the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NOif the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVENif it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

36 Morse had already been famous as an inventor before his invention of Morse code.

37 Morse waited a long time before receiving support from Congress.

38 Morse code is difficult to learn compared with other designs.

39 Companies and firms preferred to employ telegraphy operators from rural areas.
